body:
Satellites and their importance

Artificial satellites are human-made objects placed in orbit around Earth or another celestial body. They perform important functions such as communication, weather observation, navigation, scientific research and remote sensing. Remote sensing means obtaining information about an area or object from a distance, without directly touching it.

India uses satellites for television broadcasting, telecommunications, weather forecasting, disaster management and the observation of agricultural land, forests and water resources. The INSAT series is associated with communication and meteorological services, while Indian Remote Sensing satellites support Earth observation. EDUSAT was developed for educational communication.

A satellite remains in orbit because Earth's gravitational attraction continuously changes its direction of motion while it moves forward. It therefore travels around Earth instead of moving permanently in a straight line or falling directly to the ground. An ordinary satellite does not need continuous rocket thrust simply to remain in orbit, although some satellites use propulsion to adjust their paths.

Orbit: The path followed by an object as it revolves around another body under the influence of gravity. Earth's Moon is a natural satellite, whereas a spacecraft placed in orbit by humans is an artificial satellite.

Why the orbital region matters

Satellites operate at different distances from Earth. The chosen orbit affects the area a satellite can observe, how often it passes over a location and the types of services it can provide.

Low Earth orbit

Low Earth orbit (LEO) generally refers to orbital altitudes below 2,000 km. Its relative closeness to Earth makes it useful for Earth observation and many scientific missions. Satellites in LEO move rapidly around Earth rather than remaining over one fixed location. Large groups of satellites, called constellations, may work together to provide wider or more continuous coverage.

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite travels in a circular orbit above Earth's equator at an altitude of approximately 35,786 km. Its orbital period matches Earth's rotation, so it appears stationary relative to a point on the ground. This is useful for continuous communication and weather observation over a broad region.

A geosynchronous satellite has an orbital period matching Earth's rotation, but it is not necessarily geostationary. To appear fixed over one point, its orbit must also be circular and equatorial, with the satellite moving from west to east in the direction of Earth's rotation.

The meaning of space sustainability

Space sustainability means conducting space activities so that present needs can be met without seriously reducing the safety and usefulness of the space environment for future generations. Satellites provide benefits on Earth, but an increasing number of spacecraft and fragments can make some orbital regions more difficult to use safely.

The central problem is that an orbit is a shared environment. A fragment created by one mission may threaten spacecraft operated by another country or company. Safe operations therefore require cooperation, responsible behaviour during a mission and proper management when a spacecraft reaches the end of its useful life.

Space sustainability is broader than removing debris. It also includes preventing collisions, avoiding unnecessary debris generation, sharing useful safety information and planning for the safe end of a mission.

Prelims focus

  • The Moon is a natural satellite; INSAT and IRS satellites are artificial satellites.
  • Remote sensing obtains information without direct physical contact.
  • Low Earth orbit generally lies below 2,000 km.
  • Geostationary orbit is circular and equatorial, at approximately 35,786 km altitude.
  • Trap: Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not every geosynchronous orbit is geostationary.

[Sources: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 1: The Earth in the Solar System, printed pp. 4–6; NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 17: Stars and the Solar System, printed pp. 225–227 and 232–233; NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 10: Gravitation, printed pp. 131–132; European Space Agency, Types of orbits, sections on Low Earth orbit and Geostationary orbit, accessed 4 November 2026.]

title: Space Sustainability: Why Earth's Orbits Must Remain Usable

body:
What is space debris?

Space debris, also called orbital debris or space junk, consists of non-functional human-made objects and fragments that remain in orbit. Such objects no longer serve a useful operational purpose but may continue moving around Earth.

Common sources of orbital debris include:

  • Defunct satellites: Spacecraft that have stopped functioning but remain in orbit.
  • Discarded rocket stages: Parts of launch vehicles left in orbit after completing their task.
  • Fragmentation debris: Pieces produced when a satellite or rocket body breaks apart or collides with another object.
  • Small released materials: Items such as detached components and paint fragments.

It is important to distinguish debris from a working spacecraft. A functioning satellite is part of the population of objects in orbit, but it is not classified as orbital debris merely because it occupies space.

Natural objects are different

Meteoroids are naturally occurring pieces of material moving through space. When a meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere and creates a visible streak of light, the phenomenon is called a meteor. If part of it reaches the ground, that surviving material is called a meteorite.

Natural meteoroids can also threaten spacecraft, but the standard meaning of orbital debris refers to non-functional human-made material.

Why even small debris is dangerous

Objects in low Earth orbit commonly travel at speeds of several kilometres per second; typical orbital speeds are about 7–8 km per second. When 2 objects approach one another, their relative speed can also be extremely high, depending on the directions of their motion.

Because of these speeds, a small fragment can damage a satellite, solar panel or spacecraft window. Larger objects can cause severe collisions. The danger is not determined by the size of the object alone: its speed and the circumstances of impact also matter.

The large volume of space does not eliminate this risk. Satellites occupy particular orbital regions, and some of those regions contain many active spacecraft and pieces of debris. Even if 2 objects are very small compared with the space around them, their paths may bring them dangerously close.

How a collision can create further danger

A collision may break an object into many fragments. Some fragments can remain in orbit and later pass close to other satellites. A further collision may generate additional fragments, increasing the danger to spacecraft that were not involved in the original event.

In 2009, the operational Iridium 33 satellite and the non-operational Cosmos 2251 satellite collided in orbit, generating additional debris. The event demonstrates why an inactive spacecraft can remain a hazard long after it stops providing a service.

The Kessler syndrome

Kessler syndrome: A possible process in which collisions among objects in orbit produce debris that causes further collisions, creating a self-sustaining increase in the debris population.

The Kessler syndrome describes a possible long-term development of a crowded orbital environment. It does not mean that every collision automatically starts an uncontrollable chain reaction or that all orbital regions have already become unusable.

Consequences for Earth and space activities

Debris may damage spacecraft, interrupt communication or observation services, threaten astronauts and increase the effort needed to operate satellites safely. Large abandoned objects may also pose risks during atmospheric reentry. Many pieces burn up in the atmosphere, but some larger or more resistant components can survive and reach the ground.

The European Space Agency's Space Environment Report 2026, published on 14 September 2026 using observations through the end of 2025, documented continuing growth in space traffic and debris-related concerns. It reported more than 4,000 new payloads placed in orbit during 2025. New payloads are not the same as new debris: many of these spacecraft were launched for useful operations.

Prelims focus

  • Orbital debris consists of non-functional human-made objects and fragments in orbit.
  • Defunct satellites and discarded rocket bodies are important sources of debris.
  • Meteoroids are natural objects, not human-made orbital debris.
  • High orbital speeds make even small fragments dangerous.
  • Kessler syndrome refers to a potential collision-driven increase in debris.
  • Trap: A close approach is not necessarily a collision, and an active satellite is not automatically debris.

[Sources: NASA, Orbital Debris Program Office, Frequently Asked Questions, sections on orbital debris, its sources, orbital speeds and collisions, accessed 4 November 2026; European Space Agency, Space Environment Report 2026, published 14 September 2026, sections on growth trends and the Kessler syndrome, data through 31 December 2025; NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 17: Stars and the Solar System, printed pp. 232–233, for the distinction between natural objects and artificial satellites.]

title: Space Debris: Sources, Collisions and the Kessler Syndrome

body:
Space situational awareness

Satellites cannot be operated safely by considering only their own paths. Operators also need information about other spacecraft, abandoned rocket bodies and fragments that might come close to them.

Space Situational Awareness (SSA) is the knowledge of objects and conditions in space that may affect space operations. For debris safety, it includes detecting and tracking objects, estimating their orbits and assessing possible close approaches.

Ground-based radars and optical telescopes can observe many objects in orbit. Their observations help specialists estimate where those objects are likely to travel. These estimates are useful because operators cannot safely respond to an unknown hazard.

However, not every fragment can be tracked. Very small debris may be below the detection capability of available systems. An estimate of an object's future position also contains uncertainty.

Conjunction assessment and collision avoidance

A conjunction occurs when 2 orbiting objects are predicted to pass close to each other. A conjunction warning is not proof that the objects will collide. It indicates that their predicted paths require examination.

Operators assess the possible separation between the objects, the uncertainty in their predicted positions and the potential consequences of a collision. If the risk is sufficiently serious and the spacecraft has suitable control capability, the operator may change its orbit to reduce the chance of impact.

This action is called a collision-avoidance manoeuvre. It is a protective response to a particular risk. It does not remove all debris from space, and a satellite that cannot manoeuvre may have limited options.

Preventing debris generation

The most effective long-term approach is to avoid creating unnecessary debris in the first place. Space missions can reduce debris by preventing accidental releases, avoiding destructive break-ups, conducting safe operations and planning how to dispose of spacecraft after their work ends.

Another important measure is passivation. After a spacecraft or rocket stage has completed its mission, remaining stored energy is made safe where feasible. For example, reducing residual fuel pressure or discharging batteries can decrease the chance of an accidental explosion that would create fragments. Passivation reduces one source of risk; it does not itself remove an object from orbit.

What happens at the end of a mission?

Leaving every satellite in its working orbit indefinitely would increase congestion. The appropriate disposal method depends partly on where the spacecraft operates.

Disposal from low Earth orbit

A satellite in LEO may be moved into an orbit from which atmospheric drag helps it descend, or it may undergo a planned reentry. Atmospheric drag is the resisting effect of the very thin upper atmosphere on an orbiting body. It gradually reduces orbital energy and can eventually lead to reentry.

Reentry is not automatically risk-free. Some components may survive heating, so responsible disposal also considers possible risks on the ground.

Disposal near geostationary orbit

Geostationary satellites operate too high above Earth for atmospheric drag to provide a practical quick-disposal method. Instead, an old spacecraft can be moved into a graveyard orbit above the operational geostationary region and then passivated.

The purpose is to reduce interference with operational satellites while leaving the retired spacecraft in a separate orbital region.

Mitigation and removal are not the same

Debris mitigation means reducing the creation of new debris and limiting the future risk from spacecraft and rocket stages. Collision avoidance, passivation and planned disposal are examples.

Active debris removal means deliberately removing an existing piece of debris from a hazardous orbit. It is being investigated and developed because preventing new debris may not be sufficient to deal with the large amount of material already present.

Neither method guarantees that an orbit will become completely free of hazards. Space sustainability requires several complementary measures rather than a single solution.

Prelims focus

  • SSA involves detecting, tracking and assessing objects and hazards in space.
  • A conjunction is a predicted close approach; it does not necessarily mean a collision.
  • Collision avoidance changes a spacecraft's path to reduce a particular risk.
  • Passivation reduces stored energy and the risk of accidental fragmentation.
  • LEO disposal may use atmospheric reentry; GEO disposal may use a higher graveyard orbit.
  • Trap: Tracking debris does not remove it, and passivation does not itself cause deorbiting.

[Sources: NASA, Orbital Debris Program Office, Frequently Asked Questions, sections on detection, tracking, debris hazards and mitigation, accessed 4 November 2026; European Space Agency, Space Environment Report 2026, published 14 September 2026, sections on reentry, mitigation and active debris removal; United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, Guidelines for the Long-term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities, section on safety of space operations, adopted 2019, accessed 4 November 2026.]
